etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English forecasten, forcasten, equivalent to fore- +‎ cast. The noun is from Middle English forecast, forcast.

definitions.definition: To estimate how something will be in the future.

quote.citation: 2020 May 6, Graeme Pickering, “Borders Railway: time for the next step”, in Rail, page 52:
quote.text: Within six months, the total number of passengers forecast to use the line in the entire first year (650,000) had already been passed. For the first 12 months, the figure was in excess of 1.2 million. And overall, it has grown year-on-year, reaching over two million in 2018-19.

definitions.definition: To foreshadow; to suggest something in advance.

quote.citation: 1626 (date written), John Milton, “At a Vacation Exercise in the Colledge, […]”, in Poems, &c. upon Several Occasions, London:  […]  Tho[mas] Dring […], published 1673, →OCLC, page 64:
quote.text: And, if it happen as I did forecaſt, / The dainteſt diſhes ſhall be ſerv'd up laſt.

quote.citation: 2024 April 19, Charles Hugh Smith, Living on Uneasy Street‎[1]:
quote.text: It's nice to anticipate sunny weather, but it's a good idea to carry an umbrella just in case the forecasts prove overly optimistic.

definitions.definition: An estimation of a future condition.
